demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure

Maladaptive Strategies.value: keep mind occupied all the time

Threat.value: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't trust that I will do the right thing
My life has been destroyed by the trauma
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within Memory, 'Feels Present Not Past' and 'Full Sensory Reliving' indicate highly intrusive, poorly contextualized trauma memory, which conflicts with 'Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.' These can sometimes coexist, but stated this strongly they pull in opposite directions and are hard to reconcile as the same memory profile.

issues.item: Threat: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
issues.explanation: The Threat items depict pervasive fear of being physically attacked by other people ('watch other people closely', 'back to wall', 'stay alert at night'), which does not fit well with the trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another. For this trauma, threat is more plausibly guilt, condemnation, or fear of consequences, not generalized interpersonal danger.

issues.item: Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: 'Mirror Checking' is not well linked to the rest of the profile. Nothing in Triggers, Memory, Threat, or Negative Appraisals suggests appearance-focused concern, dissociation needing visual reassurance, or checking for injury; as selected, it appears clinically disconnected.

Mirror checking is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another; it more strongly suggests concerns about visible injury, appearance, or being followed, none of which are supported by the other nodes.

issues.item: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: Back-to-wall hypervigilance and scanning the room imply an interpersonal or attack-related threat context. That is difficult to integrate with the rest of the profile, which centers on guilt, reliving, and self-blame after accidentally injuring someone rather than danger from other people.

vignette:
Michael was thirty-four and had been a school counselor for nearly a decade when the accident happened. He was driving home from work on a rainy October evening, his mind already half-turned to the stack of progress notes waiting on his desk. A cyclist came out of the glare of oncoming headlights; Michael swerved too late. The impact was a sound he still hears as a wet, hollow thud, and the smell of hot asphalt and brake fluid and something metallic that he later learned was blood. He remembers kneeling on the wet road, the cyclist's leg bent at an angle that made his own stomach drop, and the man's eyes-open but unfocused, looking at nothing. The paramedics arrived, the police took his statement, and for weeks afterward he checked news sites obsessively until he found a brief update: the cyclist had survived but would never walk again. Michael had broken both his legs.

In the months that followed, Michael's life began to shrink. He could not stop thinking about the event, but he also could not think about it without his chest tightening and a wave of heat washing over him, as though his body were reliving the crash completely: the screech of tires, the jolt through the steering column, the weight of his own foot pressing the brake too late. At night, he lay rigid in bed, his ears tuned to every creak and distant siren because some part of him was convinced that if he relaxed he would miss something-a threat, an approaching danger-though he could never name what he was waiting for. He had always been a sound sleeper, but now he kept a light on, and his wife began to sleep in the guest room after the fourth time he sat bolt upright at 2 a.m., insisting he had heard a crash. The memory did not feel like a memory. It felt like it was happening now-right now, again-and when it came, all of his senses flooded: the cold rain on his face, the wet smell of rubber and exhaust, the terrible softness of the body against the car. And yet when his wife asked him what happened, he found he could not hold the whole thing in his mind at once. The words slipped away. He knew the facts, but to speak them aloud made his throat close, and he would end up staring at the wall until she stopped asking.

He began to keep his mind occupied at all costs. At work, he took on extra responsibilities-volunteering to lead the anti-bullying assembly, offering to cover for the school nurse during lunch-anything that kept him moving and talking. In the quiet gaps between student appointments, his thoughts would drift back to the intersection, the glare, the man on the ground, and so he learned to never have a quiet gap. He avoided thinking about the event with the same mechanical vigilance that he used to steer clear of the police department. He no longer drove past the local precinct; he took a longer route to work that added fifteen minutes each way, because the sight of a cruiser made his palms sweat and his stomach clench. But it was not only direct reminders that set him off. On days when his caseload felt overwhelming-when a parent yelled at him over the phone about a child's failing grades, or when he had to mediate a heated argument between two students-the pressure built in his chest, and suddenly he was back on that wet road, his hands trembling as if he were gripping the steering wheel again, his heart hammering for no visible reason. The stress itself had become a trigger, and he could not predict when it would hit.

Medical procedures became a particular kind of terror. When he took a student to the school nurse's office for a routine eye exam, the faint antiseptic smell hit him and he had to excuse himself, gasping, certain he was about to see that man on the stretcher again. He felt the crash in his body-his heart race, his skin go cold, a tremor in his hands-and he could not stop himself from scanning the room for an exit, as though he himself were in danger. He had come to believe that he could not trust himself to do the right thing. The accident had proved it: he had acted, and his actions had destroyed a stranger's life. So now he hesitated before every decision, large and small. Should he call a parent about a struggling student? Should he schedule a follow-up meeting? Every choice felt heavy with the possibility that he would make the wrong one, and that someone else would pay for it. His life, he felt certain, had been ruined by ten seconds of inattention. He had been a good husband, a decent counselor, a man who tried to help people. Now he was the man who broke another man's legs and left him in a wheelchair. There was no going back.

What finally brought Michael to seek help was a morning in late February. He had been sitting in his office, staring at a note from his wife that said she was thinking of moving into her sister's place for a while. He had barely noticed her pack a bag the night before. He was too exhausted, too locked inside the replay of the crash, too busy filling every waking minute with tasks so he would not have to feel the shame and guilt that sat in his chest like a stone. That morning, he looked at the clock and realized he could not remember a single conversation from the past week. He was afraid that he was disappearing into himself, and he was equally afraid that if he stopped trying to distract himself, the memory would swallow him whole. He wanted to find a way to trust his own hands again, to sleep in the same bed as his wife, to walk through his day without the smell of rain and rubber clinging to his lungs. He did not know if he deserved that, but he knew he could not go on as he was.
